short: A short reign of poor health and party politics, with the crown prince as regent from 1921.
full:
Yoshihito succeeded his father in July 1912. He had suffered a brain illness in infancy — usually described as meningitis — and had never been robust. His public role shrank steadily: reports of erratic behaviour at the opening of the Diet in 1913 circulated widely, he stopped appearing at official functions after 1919, and in November 1921 his son Hirohito was appointed regent. He died at the Hayama villa on 25 December 1926.

The political history of his fourteen years belongs to his ministers and the Diet rather than to him, and the weakness of the throne is part of why. Japan entered the First World War on the Allied side and took German possessions in China and the Pacific; nationwide rice riots in 1918 brought down a cabinet and produced the first commoner prime minister, Hara Takashi; the Great Kantō Earthquake killed over a hundred thousand people in 1923; and universal male suffrage was enacted in 1925, paired with a Peace Preservation Law that criminalised dissent. The era is remembered as Taishō democracy.
